title: TPM connector, BYOK & data residency review with Arbor Genomics
summary: Discovery-style security review focused on Redwood's options for BYOK (Bring Your Own Key), TPM-based connectors for on-prem key material, HSM requirements, and data residency constraints for a genomics customer. Discussed envelope encryption, key wrapping, key rotation cadence, attestation, and audit logging. Agreed on follow-ups: security whitepaper, HSM architecture diagram, and pilot plan for BYOK import with test key and attestation procedure.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Diaz (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Roth (Arbor CISO), Samir Gupta (Arbor Infra), Nora Kim (Legal), Ethan Park (SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick security review to validate Redwood's BYOK options, HSM/TPM connectors, and data residency controls for an on-prem sensitive genomics workflow.

[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the account. With me is Carlos from our SE team. We're hoping to walk through BYOK options, some TPM connector-ish patterns, and how we handle keys and logs.

[00:00:18] Lena: Thanks. High level, we process patient sequencing data. So PII/PHI controls and regional residency are non-negotiable. Key questions: can keys stay on-prem, do you support HSM-backed keys, and what attestation do you provide.

[00:00:42] Carlos: Great, and we covered some of this in the questionnaire. Two main modes: 1) Redwood-managed KMS with customer-managed keys (CMEK) where you import keys or 2) a connector model where your on-prem HSM or TPM does signing/wrapping and Redwood never holds raw key material. Both use envelope encryption on our side.

[00:01:05] Samir: Quick clarification — when you say 'TPM connector' do you mean a lightweight agent that calls our HSM, or something that holds keys locally?

[00:01:17] Carlos: The connector typically proxies wrap/unwrap operations. For TPM specifically we support a connector that uses the TPM to perform wrapping operations and returns only wrapped keys to Redwood. So the raw key material never leaves your environment. It's a key wrapping workflow; we call it the TPM/HSM proxy flow.

[00:01:40] Nora: From legal, we need to know about key escrow and the ability to compel key handover. Do you offer escrow or split-key models?

[00:01:52] Maya: Good question. By default we do not escrow cust keys. We support import and attestation via HSM (FIPS 140-2/3), and the customer controls the root key lifecycle. For customers wanting escrow, that's a negotiated feature with an audited process.

[00:02:12] Ethan: Are audit logs tamper-evident? We need proof all unwraps are logged with request metadata and retained for 7 years.

[00:02:24] Carlos: We emit structured audit logs for every crypto operation. Logs include request id, model id, actor identity (subject via SSO), and key identifier. We also stream logs to customer destinations — syslog, S3, or your SIEM. We have append-only log features and can sign log batches to provide tamper evidence.

[00:02:50] Lena: Can you show the attestation flow for HSM-backed keys? We need proof the key is in an HSM, vendor attestation, and that Redwood can't extract it.

[00:03:03] Carlos: Sure. For HSM we support three attestation modes: hardware attestation via vendor certs (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Key Vault with HSM, and external Thales/Entrust devices), remote attestation (for partners that support it), and signed import tokens. The flow: you generate a wrapping key in your HSM, export a wrapped DEK (data encryption key), send us the wrapped blob plus attestation cert chain. Our import pipeline verifies the chain and stores only the wrapped blob. We can also run a challenge-response to verify freshness.

[00:03:45] Samir: Sounds good, but we need the lookup on cross-region replication. Our data will live in EU and APAC. How do you handle key residency if runtime is multi-region?

[00:03:58] Maya: We have region-tagged key policies. You can pin keys to regions so that unwrapping occurs only in the region you authorize. For cross-region requests we can either route the request to the key's region or use customer-approved key replication (you replicate the key material between your HSMs, not Redwood). That avoids us holding the key in multiple regions.

[00:04:20] Nora: Any SOC 2 or ISO docs we can review? We need SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence, plus penetration test reports redacted.

[00:04:30] Maya: Yes, we have a security pack. I'll send SOC 2 Type II and ISO attestations. Pen tests are redacted but include high-level findings. We'll add links after the call.

[00:04:45] Ethan: For the TPM connector — what network requirements are there? We try to avoid long-lived connections from our HSM to the cloud.

[00:04:56] Carlos: The connector is designed to be outbound-only over TLS, uses mTLS for client certs, and can be co-located in your VPC. It supports ephemeral sessions. You can place an egress proxy that only allows the connector to talk to Redwood's ingestion endpoints.

[00:05:12] Lena: What about key rotation? We have strict rotation policies — monthly on some classes. Can you automate rotation without re-encrypting all object store data?

[00:05:24] Carlos: Envelope encryption helps here. We rotate the KEK (key encryption key) and issue new DEKs for new objects. For existing objects you can opt for lazy re-encrypt (on-read) or run a bulk rewrap job. We provide tooling for rewrap; it's a customer-triggered operation and can be done with your HSM so raw keys never leave your control.

[00:05:46] Samir: Does Redwood store DEKs in plaintext anywhere?

[00:05:51] Maya: No. DEKs are generated per object, encrypted (wrapped) with the KEK. We store only wrapped DEKs. The only place raw DEKs exist is transiently inside the HSM operation during wrap/unwrap and in-mem during processing; we do not persist plaintext DEKs.

[00:06:08] Nora: Legal also wants to know on compelled disclosure — if a lawful request comes, can Redwood be forced to provide keys?

[00:06:18] Maya: If the key material is customer-held on-prem or under your HSM, Redwood cannot produce raw keys. If you import keys into a Redwood-managed KMS and negotiate escrow, that’s different. We will always notify customers per our policy unless prohibited. Details in the data protection addendum.

[00:06:39] Carlos: Quick demo note: we can do a lightweight POC where we import a test wrapped key and show unwrapping only occurs in a pinned region. That gives you the evidence for routing + attestation.

[00:06:55] Lena: Perfect. Also need to confirm SSO / RBAC mapping — engineers must not be able to request unwrapping unless role-based policy allows.

[00:07:06] Carlos: We integrate with SAML/OIDC SSO. RBAC maps SSO groups to roles; key policies can reference roles to authorize unwraps. We also support time-limited grants and just-in-time approval flows.

[00:07:22] Ethan: About logs and integrity — you mentioned signing log batches. Is there a chain-of-trust we can verify?

[00:07:29] Carlos: Yes — we can sign log batches with a signing key and provide the verification public key for you. We also support log forwarding into your SIEM with TLS and mutual auth, so you can retain logs in your region for regulatory needs.

[00:07:47] Maya: Side note: some customers use HSMs with split control where two officers have to approve key imports. We can map that process into our onboarding via manual attestation steps.

[00:07:58] Nora: That would be necessary for certain datasets.

[00:08:05] Samir: What's the failure/fallback model? If your region goes down, can we failover to a secondary region without exposing keys?

[00:08:15] Carlos: Options: 1) Active-passive where you replicate keys between your HSMs and change routing to the secondary region, 2) Redwood can keep replicas of wrapped keys only if you allow it and you maintain control of KEKs, or 3) a cold recovery flow where a new key is imported into a secondary HSM — all documented in DR runbooks. We'll share runbook samples.

[00:08:40] Lena: On attestation — what standards do you rely on? FIPS, Common Criteria? We need clear cert references.

[00:08:48] Carlos: FIPS 140-2/3 for HSM modules, and we can provide vendor attestation docs. For TPM, we rely on TCG attestation models. We'll include public cert chains in the whitepaper.

[00:09:05] Ethan: Are there performance impacts for using an on-prem HSM or TPM connector? We run models with low tail-latency SLOs.

[00:09:15] Carlos: Envelope encryption minimizes per-token crypto. Most operations use cached DEKs and KV caches on the runtime. Unwrap calls are only needed when a DEK isn't present; we recommend warm cache patterns and pre-warming DEKs for low-latency routes. The connector adds a small ms overhead on initial unwraps; we can benchmark with your workload.

[00:09:42] Maya: We should capture a small benchmark: sample workload, typical sequence lengths, and desired p99 latency. Carlos can set up a run with a wrapped test key.

[00:09:55] Lena: Ok. One more — data residency: we need to ensure logs and any metadata that could identify subjects stay in EU for EU-tenants. Is that configurable?

[00:10:06] Carlos: Yes. You can configure data-plane region, log ingestion target, and metadata retention. We support per-tenant policies so logs and artifacts stay in your chosen region.

[00:10:18] Nora: Contractually we will list geographic controls in the DPA.

[00:10:24] Maya: Good. Quick run-through of next steps and owners at the end.

--- Midcall deep dive notes ---

[00:10:45] Carlos: Let's walk a concrete import example — I'll read a sample flow. Step 1: generate KEK inside customer's HSM or TPM. Step 2: create a DEK, wrap with KEK. Step 3: send wrapped DEK + attestation cert chain + manifest to Redwood. Step 4: Redwood verifies and stores wrapped DEK. Wrap metadata includes algorithm (e.g., AES-256-GCM), key id, creation epoch.

[00:11:18] Samir: What about algorithm constraints? We require AES-GCM or XChaCha20 for some pipelines.

[00:11:24] Carlos: We support AES-256-GCM and XChaCha20-Poly1305 for DEKs. KEKs should be RSA-OAEP- based wrap or AES-KW per your HSM capabilities. We'll include supported cipher suites.

[00:11:40] Lena: How do you prove you can't extract keys? We need some kind of zero-knowledge proof or attestation.

[00:11:49] Carlos: Attestation plus walled-off import pipeline. For many HSM vendors, the hardware attestation cert asserts keys are non-exportable. We also offer live challenge where Redwood requests an HSM to sign a nonce to prove possession without revealing the key.

[00:12:05] Maya: Also note legal protections — contract language that Redwood will not persist or export raw keys and will only perform operations per key policy.

[00:12:15] Nora: We'll want that SLA and contractual language.

[00:12:21] Maya: We'll include a draft DPA clause and example language.

[00:12:27] Ethan: For the connector, is there an open-source implementation we can review?

[00:12:33] Carlos: We have a reference connector repo (internal) and a sanitized OSS sample we can share. It's not productionized for all HSM vendors but shows the handshake and mTLS flows. I'll link it.

[00:12:45] Lena: Benchmarks — can we get token-level latency numbers with an on-prem HSM flow?

[00:12:52] Carlos: Yes. We'll run a microbenchmark. Ideally we'll get a small sample that mimics your seq length distributions.

[00:13:00] Maya: Quick Q from Nora: are your KMS operations auditable via a third-party auditor?

[00:13:06] Carlos: Audit logs are exportable and we allow auditors read-only access under NDA — we can carve that into the audit process.

[00:13:15] Samir: Any rate limits on unwraps? If model farm spikes we don't want unwrap throttling to become the bottleneck.

[00:13:24] Carlos: There are operational safeguards; we recommend caching DEKs at the runtime with TTLs. For high-throughput customers we set up pre-warming and batching to reduce unwrap QPS to HSM. If needed, we support burst allowances on dedicated capacity.

[00:13:45] Lena: We also need to understand retention for keys and logs once a contract ends.

[00:13:51] Maya: We have data retention and key deletion playbooks. On termination you can request key destruction and a signed destruction certificate. Logs retention is configurable. We'll supply the deletion certificate template.

[00:14:06] Nora: Good. One last legal ask: if we use Redwood-managed KMS with imported keys, will Redwood ever assist in key recovery?

[00:14:14] Maya: We can assist in recovery workflows only if you grant us explicit recovery access during onboarding; otherwise, recovery is with your HSM. We'll document options.

[00:14:26] Carlos: Wrapping up the technical checklist: attestation types, cipher suites, region pinning, log forwarding, connector network model, rotation cadence, and runbook.

[00:14:40] Lena: Can you send an architecture diagram showing where keys live in each model?

[00:14:45] Maya: Absolutely — we'll include sample diagrams in the whitepaper.

--- Final recap / next steps ---

[00:14:52] Maya: To recap: 1) We'll send the BYOK/HSM technical whitepaper and SOC2/ISO artifacts (Maya). 2) Carlos will prepare a TPM connector POC script and a benchmark plan. 3) Lena will provide residency regs and policy constraints. 4) We'll schedule the POC and a deeper SE-led bench the week of April 12.

[00:15:12] Lena: Sounds good. Thank you.

[00:15:16] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.

[00:15:20] (call ends)

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (TEE heard as T-E-E), and 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash'. Some speaker labels may be generic.
